system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Paxos
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The proposer/accepter/learner protocol with prepare/ack/accept! phases and proposal numbers. Covers why overlapping majorities give safety (agreement, validity), why termination needs a single stable proposer or leader, and the multi-Paxos replicated state machine optimization. Excludes Raft implementation details.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C02-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: In Paxos, processes are classified as proposers, accepters, and learners (one process may hold all three roles), and a proposer tries to ratify a proposed value by collecting acceptances from a majority of the accepters, with learners observing the ratification.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0127-s07] Processes are classiﬁed as proposers, accepters, and learners (a single process may have all three roles).
    [CS-DIST-p0127-s08] The idea is that a proposer attempts to ratify a proposed decision value (from an arbitrary input set) by collecting acceptances from a majority of the accepters, and this ratiﬁcation is observed by the learners.
- CS-DIST-C02-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Basic Paxos is a one-shot algorithm that solves a single agreement problem, whereas multi-Paxos uses repeated executions of basic Paxos to implement a replicated state machine.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0126-s09] This is a one-shot version of Paxos that solves a single agreement problem.
    [CS-DIST-p0126-s10] The version that is more typically used, called multi-Paxos, uses repeated executions of the basic Paxos algorithm to implement a replicated state machine; we’ll describe this in §12.7.
- CS-DIST-C02-S1-03.r1a | S3
  ATOM: The algorithm described runs in a message-passing model with asynchrony and fewer than $n/2$ crash failures.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0126-s14] The algorithm runs in a message-passing model with asynchrony and fewer than n/2 crash failures (but not Byzantine failures, at least in the original
- CS-DIST-C02-S1-03.r1b | S3
  ATOM: The algorithm described does not tolerate Byzantine failures, at least in its original version.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0126-s14] The algorithm runs in a message-passing model with asynchrony and fewer than n/2 crash failures (but not Byzantine failures, at least in the original
- CS-DIST-C02-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: In Paxos, after a proposer has received ack messages from a majority of accepters, it sets its value v to the value in the ack with the highest proposal number if any ack contained a value, and then sends accept!(r, v) to the accepters.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0128-s13] The proposer waits (possibly forever) to receive ack from a majority of accepters.
    [CS-DIST-p0128-s14] If any ack contained a value, it sets v to the most recent (in proposal number ordering) value that it received.
    [CS-DIST-p0128-s15] It then sends accept!(r, v) to all accepters (or just a majority).
- CS-DIST-C02-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: In multi-Paxos, if the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages between agreement instances for consecutive operations can be skipped, reducing the time to certify each operation to a single round-trip of accept! and accepted messages.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0135-s04] If the proposer doesn’t change very often, a further optimization allows skipping the prepare and ack messages in between agreement protocols for consecutive operations.
    [CS-DIST-p0135-s05] This reduces the time to certify each operation to a single round-trip for the accept! and accepted messages, which is about the best we can reasonably hope for.
- CS-DIST-C02-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Paxos preserves a value accepted in an earlier round because a majority of accepters that accepted it in round r and a majority that acknowledge in a later round r′ must overlap, so the overlapping accepter reports the round-r value to the round-r′ proposer, and by induction that value becomes the proposal value in all later rounds that get past the acknowledgment stage.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0130-s10] The second trick is to use overlapping majorities to make sure that any value that is accepted is not lost.
    [CS-DIST-p0130-s11] If the only way to decide on a value in round r is to get a majority of accepters to accept it, and the only way to make progress in round r′ is to get acknowledgments from a majority of accepters, these two majorities overlap.
    [CS-DIST-p0130-s12] So in particular the overlapping process reports the round-r proposal value to the proposer in round r′, and we can show by induction on r′ that this round-r proposal value becomes the proposal value in all subsequent rounds that proceed past the acknowledgment stage.
- CS-DIST-C02-S2-04 | S2
  ATOM: In Paxos, a proposer first sends prepare(r) with proposal number r to the accepters, and an accepter replies with ack(r, v, rv) only if r is greater than both the highest proposal number it has already responded to with an ack and the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, where v and rv are the value and number of the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted (or ⊥ and −∞ if none).
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0128-s05] The proposer sends a message prepare(r) to all accepters.
    [CS-DIST-p0128-s08] Each accepter compares r to the highest-numbered proposal for which it has responded to a prepare message and the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted.
    [CS-DIST-p0128-s09] If r is greater than both, it responds with ack(r, v, rv), where v is the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted and rv is the number of that proposal (or ⊥and −∞if there is no such proposal).
- CS-DIST-C02-S3-01.r1 | S2
  ATOM: The solution described for Paxos is to ensure that there is eventually some interval during which exactly one proposer exists and does not fail.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0133-s17] The solution is to ensure that there is eventually some interval during which there is exactly one proposer who doesn’t fail.
- CS-DIST-C02-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Without additional assumptions, Paxos guarantees only its safety properties (validity and agreement) and does not guarantee termination.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0132-s05] We consider only the safety properties of the protocol, corresponding to validity and agreement.
    [CS-DIST-p0132-s06] Without additional assumptions, Paxos does not guarantee termination.
- CS-DIST-C02-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Because a leader election mechanism of the kind Paxos needs for progress would allow consensus to be solved, the FLP result implies it cannot be built using only the tools of the asynchronous message-passing model.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0134-s07] Since implementing this kind of leader election allows us to solve consensus, the FLP result (Chapter 11) implies that we can’t build it using only the tools available in the asynchronous message-passing model.
- CS-DIST-C02-S3-04 | S3
  ATOM: When there are multiple proposers in Paxos they can step on each other. For example, two carefully synchronized proposers that alternate sending prepare messages can prevent any accepter from ever accepting, because an accepter promises not to accept accept!(r, v) once it has responded to prepare(r + 1).
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0133-s15] If there are multiple proposers, then they can step on each other.
    [CS-DIST-p0133-s16] For example, it’s enough to have two carefully-synchronized proposers alternate sending out prepare messages to prevent any accepter from every accepting (since an accepter promises not to accept accept!(r, v) once it has responded to prepare(r + 1)).
